page_title: How to Hold Your Team Accountable

summary.title: How to Hold Your Team Accountable
summary.one_liner: Learn Jonathan Raymond's five-level "accountability dial" and four management techniques (open questions, weeding out excuses, empathising instead of solving, disagree and commit) for holding a team to account.
takeaways: Accountability means providing an account of what happened; holding someone accountable means asking questions about it.
Raymond's accountability dial has five levels: Mention, Invitation, Conversation, Boundary, and Limit, and can be turned up or down as needed.
Open questions (e.g. 'What help do you need?') push people to think through issues more than yes/no requests.
Weed out excuses (causes with no personal responsibility) and prefer protective consequences that protect business and team needs over punitive ones.
summary.summary: This blog post by Dave Bailey, written for CEOs and managers, explains how to hold a team accountable without taking over their work. It defines accountability and introduces Jonathan Raymond's five-step "accountability dial" from a light Mention up to a final-warning Limit. It then covers four practices: asking open questions, weeding out excuses, empathising rather than solving problems, and the "disagree and commit" approach popularised by Jeff Bezos. The post closes with a discussion of protective versus punitive consequences and a list of possible consequences, with examples.
